categoryName: Not yet on the M1 schedule

questions.stem: A physiology researcher is tracing the sequence of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis that ends in cortisol synthesis. Which of the following hormones is secreted by the hypothalamus to initiate this cascade?

explanation.summary: The HPA axis begins with hypothalamic CRH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which activates the anterior pituitary. The pituitary then secretes ACTH, which triggers cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus, and acts downstream of CRH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid made in the adrenal gland and is not part of the CRH-ACTH-cortisol cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADH regulates water balance and is not the hormone that initiates cortisol synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol is the end product synthesized in the adrenal gland, not the initiating hypothalamic signal.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on a corticosteroid, which markedly reduces joint inflammation. Which of the following best describes how corticosteroids decrease inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They decrease production of anti-inflammatory mediators such as IL-10 and IL-4

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase production of proinflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha and IL-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit proinflammatory mediators and stimulate anti-inflammatory mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators equally

explanation.summary: Cortisol shifts the balance away from inflammation on both sides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cortisol inhibits production of proinflammatory mediators (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, IL-2, IFN-gamma, IFN-alpha, TNF-alpha) while increasing anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, IL-4, IL-13). This dual action reduces the overall inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They increase anti-inflammatory mediators rather than decreasing them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids suppress, not increase, proinflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They do not inhibit anti-inflammatory mediators; those are increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They suppress proinflammatory mediators rather than stimulating them.

questions.stem: A pediatrician wants a single-dose corticosteroid for an asthma exacerbation that has high glucocorticoid activity and a long duration of action so it can be dosed once and exert its effect for several days. Which of the following corticosteroids best fits this profile?

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone has the highest glucocorticoid activity and a long duration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dexamethasone has a relative glucocorticoid activity of 30 and a long duration of action, making it well suited for single-dose use in a pediatric asthma exacerbation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is used exclusively as a mineralocorticoid and has essentially no glucocorticoid activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrocortisone has glucocorticoid activity of 1 and a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prednisone has moderate glucocorticoid activity (4) but only an intermediate duration.

questions.stem: A physician is deciding whether corticosteroids are safe in several patients. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to corticosteroid therapy because these drugs would worsen it directly?

explanation.summary: Immunosuppression makes an untreated systemic fungal infection an absolute contraindication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids suppress the immune system, leaving the body unable to fight a systemic fungal infection, so this is an absolute contraindication to their use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diabetes can be worsened by corticosteroids, but it is a relative caution rather than an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma can be aggravated by steroids but is not an absolute contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoporosis is worsened by steroids and warrants caution but is not the absolute contraindication tested here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncontrolled hypertension warrants caution but is not an absolute contraindication.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with persistent asthma needs long-term corticosteroid therapy, and the clinician wants to minimize systemic adverse effects. Which of the following strategies best reduces the systemic effects of corticosteroids in asthma treatment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lowest effective dose for the shortest time

explanation.summary: Inhaled delivery keeps the drug in the airways and limits systemic absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids act mainly in the lungs and are minimally absorbed systemically, so they reduce systemic adverse effects while treating airway inflammation in asthma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Every-other-day dosing can lessen adrenal suppression but does not specifically limit systemic exposure the way inhaled delivery does.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intra-articular injections treat joints and are not a route used for asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Using the lowest effective dose is a general principle but does not target the airways or minimize systemic absorption as directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systemic corticosteroids actually increase systemic exposure and adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on chronic high-dose oral steroids for temporal arteritis develops new-onset hyperglycemia requiring treatment. Drugs from which of the following classes are the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus?

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids are the leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids mimic cortisol, increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and decreasing pancreatic insulin synthesis, which can cause new or worsen existing diabetes. This makes them the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes mellitus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics are not a leading cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antihistamines are not a significant cause of hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-blockers may blunt glucose recovery but are not the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NSAIDs are associated mainly with gastrointestinal adverse effects, not drug-induced diabetes.

questions.stem: Cortisol circulates at roughly 100 times the concentration of aldosterone and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with similar affinity, yet aldosterone dominates mineralocorticoid signaling in the kidney. Which of the following best explains why cortisol does not overwhelm the mineralocorticoid receptor in these tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol to cortisone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldosterone has a 100-fold higher affinity for the receptor than cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol is entirely bound to plasma proteins and cannot enter cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortisol is unable to bind the mineralocorticoid receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid receptors are located only in the central nervous system

explanation.summary: An enzyme protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol.
explanation.whyCorrect: In mineralocorticoid target tissues, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol into inactive cortisone. This 'protects' the mineralocorticoid receptor so aldosterone, rather than the far more abundant cortisol, dominates its signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The two hormones have similar receptor affinity; aldosterone does not simply out-compete cortisol by affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cortisol is not fully protein-bound; free cortisol readily enters cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cortisol does bind the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone; that is exactly the problem the enzyme solves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mineralocorticoid receptors are present in the kidney, colon, and salivary and sweat glands, not only the CNS.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents in preterm labor at 30 weeks of gestation. To accelerate fetal lung maturity and reduce neonatal respiratory complications, the obstetrician administers an intramuscular corticosteroid. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Antenatal betamethasone accelerates fetal lung development.
explanation.whyCorrect: Betamethasone given intramuscularly (12 mg, two doses 24 hours apart) for preterm labor accelerates development of type I and type II pneumocytes, improving lung mechanics and surfactant production and reducing neonatal morbidity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisone is a short-acting agent with low glucocorticoid potency and is not the antenatal agent used for lung maturity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for salt retention, not fetal lung maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, not a corticosteroid used to mature fetal lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical hydrocortisone treats skin conditions and would not reach the fetus systemically.

questions.stem: A patient is given a mineralocorticoid, which acts on the principal cells of the renal collecting duct. Which of the following best describes the net effect of aldosterone at this site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased reabsorption of both sodium and potassium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased free water excretion with no change in sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased sodium excretion and increased potassium reabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sodium reabsorption and increased potassium excretion

explanation.summary: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and wastes potassium in the collecting duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption by upregulating luminal sodium channels and the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. The pump drives potassium into the cell, and increased potassium channels then secrete it into the urine, so the net effect is sodium reabsorption with potassium excretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption rather than decreasing transport of both ions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone acts on sodium and potassium handling, not calcium and phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium reabsorption drives concurrent water reabsorption, expanding plasma volume, not free water excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and excretes potassium, the opposite of this choice.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who has taken high-dose prednisone for a year after a kidney transplant abruptly stops the medication. Over the next two days he develops fatigue, nausea, and profound hypotension. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

explanation.summary: Abrupt steroid withdrawal after chronic use precipitates adrenal crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolonged exogenous corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, leading to adrenal suppression and inadequate endogenous cortisol production. Sudden discontinuation unmasks adrenal insufficiency, which is why corticosteroids are tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis occurs on exposure to a drug, not on its discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cushing syndrome results from excess, not deficient, corticosteroid effect and would not follow abrupt withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia, not hypotension after steroid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steroids raise blood glucose while being taken; stopping them would not cause hypotension and these symptoms.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been taking prednisone and recently added regular ibuprofen for joint pain. She now presents with epigastric pain and melena. The concurrent use of these two drugs most notably increases her risk of which of the following adverse effects?

explanation.summary: Steroids plus NSAIDs sharply raise the risk of ulcers and GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids increase gastric acid secretion and predispose to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. This risk increases nearly four-fold when they are combined with NSAIDs, which fits this patient's epigastric pain and melena.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal suppression relates to prolonged systemic steroid exposure, not to NSAID co-administration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glaucoma is a steroid effect on the eye and is unrelated to combining steroids with NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral thrush is linked to inhaled corticosteroids, not to the steroid-NSAID combination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoporosis is a long-term steroid effect but is not specifically potentiated by adding an NSAID.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy using an inhaled corticosteroid daily for asthma develops white, curd-like plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off to reveal an erythematous base. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Inhaled steroids predispose to oral Candida infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce the local immune response in the mouth and throat, allowing opportunistic Candida albicans to cause oral thrush, which presents as removable white plaques. Rinsing the mouth after each inhaler use helps prevent it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aphthous ulcers are shallow painful ulcers, not white curd-like plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpetic stomatitis produces painful vesicles and ulcers, not scrapable white plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukoplakia forms adherent white patches that do not scrape off and is not caused by inhaled steroids in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lichen planus produces lacy white striae that are fixed, not removable plaques from steroid use.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with stable angina takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet during an episode of exertional chest pain, and his symptoms resolve within minutes. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism by which this drug relieves his chest pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes beta-adrenergic receptors on the myocardium

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases heart rate and contractility to improve perfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits platelet aggregation within the coronary arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is converted to nitric oxide

explanation.summary: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP to relax vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the body, nitrates are converted to nitric oxide (NO). NO activates guanylyl cyclase, which increases cGMP and causes relaxation (dilation) of vascular smooth muscle. This vasodilation is the basis for the anti-anginal effect of nitrates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-blockade is not the mechanism of nitrates and is not described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium-channel blockade is the mechanism of a different drug class; nitrates act through the NO/cGMP pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrates reduce cardiac workload; they do not primarily increase heart rate and contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the anti-anginal effect to vasodilation, not to antiplatelet action.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is treated with nitroglycerin for angina. The drug reduces her myocardial oxygen demand. Which of the following effects most directly accounts for this reduction in oxygen demand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reflex increase in myocardial contraction force

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increase in heart rate to improve tissue perfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: An increase in systemic vascular resistance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dilation of the large veins returning to the heart

explanation.summary: Nitrate-induced venodilation lowers the work of the heart and reduces myocardial oxygen use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that relaxation (dilation) of the large veins that return to the heart decreases contraction force, increases blood flow, and reduces myocardial oxygen use. Lowering the workload of the heart in this way decreases its oxygen demand and relieves ischemic chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitrates decrease contraction force; they do not reflexively increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing heart rate would raise, not lower, myocardial oxygen demand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrates cause vasodilation and lower vascular resistance rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrates dilate coronary arteries; they do not constrict them.

questions.stem: In addition to reducing the heart's oxygen demand, nitrates relieve angina through an effect that increases oxygen supply to the myocardium. Which of the following best describes this additional effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An increase in blood hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constriction of peripheral veins to raise coronary perfusion pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dissolution of atherosclerotic plaque within the coronary arteries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of new coronary vessel growth

explanation.summary: Nitrates also cause direct coronary artery vasodilation, increasing oxygen supply to the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond lowering oxygen demand through venodilation, the brick notes that nitrates cause some direct coronary artery vasodilation that increases oxygen supply to the heart, further relieving chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitrates do not raise hemoglobin concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitrates dilate veins rather than constricting them, and venoconstriction is not their mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrates relieve symptoms by vasodilation; they do not dissolve plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrates act acutely by dilating existing vessels, not by growing new ones.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man develops acute substernal chest pain in the emergency department. He is given a nitroglycerin tablet to place under his tongue. Which of the following best explains why the sublingual route is preferred for acute angina?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It automatically provides a built-in nitrate-free interval

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is effective only for chronic angina, not acute episodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is rapidly absorbed and avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is slowly absorbed, providing sustained drug levels over many hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: It undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism before reaching the circulation

explanation.summary: Sublingual nitroglycerin is absorbed rapidly and bypasses first-pass metabolism, giving fast relief of acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that sublingual nitroglycerin tablets are the most common form: placed under the tongue, they avoid first-pass metabolism, are rapidly absorbed, and can quickly relieve angina. This makes them ideal for acute episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A nitrate-free interval is a deliberate dosing strategy, not an inherent feature of a single sublingual tablet.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sublingual nitroglycerin is a short-acting agent used for acute angina.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slow, sustained absorption describes oral agents like isosorbide mononitrate, not sublingual nitroglycerin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Avoiding first-pass metabolism is precisely the advantage of the sublingual route.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic stable angina is prescribed a nitrate that is swallowed as an oral tablet, is slowly absorbed, and undergoes first-pass metabolism. Which of the following agents is he most likely taking?

explanation.summary: Oral isosorbide mononitrate is slowly absorbed, undergoes first-pass metabolism, and is used for chronic angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes isosorbide mononitrate as a delayed-release tablet that is swallowed, slowly absorbed, and undergoes first-pass metabolism. Despite this, it produces the same vasodilation effects and is used for chronic angina.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IV nitroglycerin is given intravenously and bypasses first-pass metabolism, and it is short-acting for acute use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium nitroprusside is an IV short-acting agent, not an oral tablet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sublingual nitroglycerin is placed under the tongue and avoids first-pass metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Translingual nitroglycerin is a spray applied to the tongue and is short-acting for acute angina.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with severe chest pain has received repeated doses of sublingual nitroglycerin, but her pain keeps returning after each dose wears off. The physician applies a transdermal nitroglycerin patch to her chest. Which property of the patch makes it useful in this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It avoids all systemic absorption, acting only locally on the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is indicated exclusively for chronic angina and never for acute pain

choices.label: C
choices.text: It works by a mechanism unrelated to nitric oxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its delayed onset and slower absorption through the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its immediate onset makes it faster than sublingual tablets

explanation.summary: Transdermal nitroglycerin has a delayed onset and is more slowly absorbed, giving a continuous effect useful for persistent, late acute angina.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that nitroglycerin ointment and the transdermal patch have a delayed onset because of transdermal absorption. This makes them useful for late acute angina: rather than repeatedly re-dosing sublingual nitroglycerin, applying a patch provides a continuous effect as the drug is more slowly absorbed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The patch is absorbed transdermally into the circulation to produce systemic vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In this clinical scenario the patch is used for continuing (late) acute angina, not only chronic angina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Like all nitrates, the patch works through conversion to nitric oxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patch has a delayed, not immediate, onset; sublingual tablets act faster.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is started on nitroglycerin for angina. Which of the following is the most common adverse effect he is likely to experience?

explanation.summary: Headache is the most common adverse effect of nitrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common adverse effect of nitrates is headache, reported by more than 60% of patients who receive nitroglycerin. It is thought to result from the rapid vasodilation nitroglycerin produces, and is notably less common with long-acting isosorbide mononitrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bradycardia is not described as a nitrate adverse effect in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Constipation is not a nitrate adverse effect discussed in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dry cough is associated with a different drug class, not nitrates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrates cause vasodilation and hypotension, not hypertension.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of atherosclerosis develops chest pain when he walks uphill. His physician explains that his angina pectoris is caused by which of the following underlying processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess oxygen supply to the myocardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by a thrombus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spasm of the lower esophageal sphincter

explanation.summary: Angina pectoris is chest pain caused by myocardial ischemia, a lack of oxygen reaching heart cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines angina pectoris as chest pain caused by myocardial ischemia (lack of oxygen leading toward cardiac cell death). Atherosclerosis reduces the effective diameter of blood vessels, lowering blood flow and oxygen delivery to the myocardium and producing the ischemic chest pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angina results from insufficient, not excess, oxygen delivery to the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pericardial inflammation is a different entity and is not the cause of angina described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary embolism is a separate condition and is not the described cause of angina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Esophageal spasm can mimic chest pain but is not the mechanism of angina pectoris.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is receiving intravenous nitroglycerin. Which of the following adverse effects most specifically requires that his blood pressure be monitored regularly during this therapy?

explanation.summary: IV nitrates cause significant vasodilation that can produce hypotension, so blood pressure must be monitored regularly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that IV nitroglycerin and sodium nitroprusside are used to acutely lower blood pressure, and the significant vasodilation they cause can produce hypotension. Any patient receiving nitrates should have blood pressure monitored regularly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Headache is the most common adverse effect but is not the reason blood pressure is monitored.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrate tolerance is a loss of drug effect over time, not an indication for blood-pressure monitoring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral edema is not a nitrate adverse effect discussed in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reflex bradycardia is not the monitored concern described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man whose angina is usually well controlled has now received continuous nitrate therapy for more than 14 hours without any nitrate-free period. His previously controlled chest pain has returned despite ongoing dosing. Which of the following best explains the loss of drug efficacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A paradoxical reflex vasoconstriction caused by cGMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: An IgE-mediated allergic reaction to nitrates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced conversion of nitroglycerin to nitric oxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased first-pass metabolism raising active drug levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nitrate tolerance from sustained high-dose exposure

explanation.summary: Continuous exposure to high-dose nitrates causes tolerance (tachyphylaxis), attenuating their effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that frequently repeated or continuous exposure to high doses of nitrates leads to tolerance (tachyphylaxis), a marked attenuation of most of their pharmacological effects. After more than 14 hours of continuous nitrates without a nitrate-free interval, the returning chest pain reflects developing nitrate tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cGMP mediates vasodilation; a paradoxical reflex vasoconstriction from cGMP is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the loss of effect to tolerance, not to an allergic (IgE-mediated) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance is associated with reduced, not enhanced, conversion of nitroglycerin to NO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased active drug levels would enhance, not reduce, the effect.

questions.stem: A physician wants to design a nitrate regimen that minimizes the development of tolerance in a patient on long-acting nitrate therapy. Which of the following strategies is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer the nitrate continuously without interruption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give the drug every 4 hours without any break

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include a daily 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval

choices.label: D
choices.text: Steadily increase the dose over time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch the patient to intravenous dosing around the clock

explanation.summary: A daily 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval decreases the likelihood of nitrate tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that nitrate therapy should be designed to prevent tolerance, and that nitrates require a 10-12 hour nitrate-free interval to decrease the likelihood of tolerance and allow the return of efficacy. For example, a patch is worn for 12-14 hours and removed for 10-12 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuous, uninterrupted dosing promotes tolerance rather than preventing it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Frequent dosing with no break provides continuous exposure, promoting tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose does not prevent tolerance and can worsen adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Around-the-clock IV dosing provides no nitrate-free interval and would encourage tolerance.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to describe a proposed cellular mechanism underlying nitrate tolerance. Which of the following best fits what the brick describes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reduced capacity to convert nitroglycerin to nitric oxide

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increase in intracellular cGMP production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Downregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors in the myocardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced first-pass metabolism that increases active drug delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle

explanation.summary: Nitrate tolerance may result from reduced ability of vascular smooth muscle to convert nitroglycerin to NO.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the magnitude of tolerance is a function of dosage and frequency of use, and that tolerance may result from a reduced capacity of the vascular smooth muscle to convert nitroglycerin to NO (true vascular tolerance) or from activation of mechanisms extraneous to the vessel wall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased cGMP would strengthen the response, the opposite of tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-receptor downregulation is unrelated to the nitrate NO/cGMP mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance is a pharmacodynamic loss of effect at the vessel, not increased active drug delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance reflects a diminished vasodilatory response; upregulating guanylyl cyclase would enhance, not blunt, the effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with erectile dysfunction and no correctable underlying cause is started on sildenafil. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug improves erectile function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates guanylyl cyclase to increase production of cGMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks phosphodiesterase type 5 and reduces the breakdown of cGMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly causes vasoconstriction within the corpus cavernosum

choices.label: D
choices.text: It directly stimulates nitric oxide synthase in the vascular endothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases release of nitric oxide from penile smooth muscle

explanation.summary: PDE-5 inhibitors block the enzyme that degrades cGMP, prolonging smooth muscle relaxation and blood flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under normal circumstances PDE-5 degrades cGMP, which would decrease smooth muscle relaxation and blood flow. By blocking PDE-5, these drugs reduce cGMP breakdown, leading to prolonged smooth muscle dilation in response to nitric oxide and increased blood flow in the corpus cavernosum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Guanylyl cyclase is activated by nitric oxide, not by PDE-5 inhibitors; the drugs do not increase cGMP production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drugs promote vasodilation and increased blood flow, not vasoconstriction, in the corpus cavernosum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PDE-5 inhibitors do not stimulate nitric oxide synthase; they act downstream on cGMP metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PDE-5 inhibitors do not increase nitric oxide release; they prolong the effect of cGMP already generated by the NO pathway.

questions.stem: During the normal male sexual response, nitric oxide is released and activates an enzyme that converts GTP to cGMP, leading to smooth muscle relaxation. Which enzyme is directly activated by nitric oxide?

explanation.summary: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, which converts GTP to cGMP to relax smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, which converts GTP to cGMP; the net result is relaxation of smooth muscle and increased blood flow needed for an erection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP, not cGMP, and is not the target of nitric oxide here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP3A4 is a metabolic enzyme in the liver, not part of the cGMP-generating pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide synthase produces nitric oxide; it does not convert GTP to cGMP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphodiesterase type 5 degrades cGMP rather than producing it.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man asks his physician for an erectile dysfunction medication that will give him the largest possible window of time for sexual activity after a single dose. Which of the following PDE-5 inhibitors has the longest duration of action, up to 36 hours?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All four have an equal duration of action

explanation.summary: Tadalafil has the longest duration of action, up to 36 hours, giving the widest window for sexual activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the four PDE-5 inhibitors, tadalafil has the longest time frame of efficacy, up to 36 hours, which gives the patient a much larger window for sexual activity relative to the others.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The durations differ substantially, ranging from about 4 hours for sildenafil to 36 hours for tadalafil.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Avanafil has a duration of action of about 6 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sildenafil has a duration of action of about 4 hours, the shortest of the group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vardenafil has a duration of action of about 7 hours.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man taking sublingual nitroglycerin for angina also took sildenafil earlier the same evening. He now presents with lightheadedness and a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains this dangerous interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct vasoconstriction of coronary arteries causing ischemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive increase in cardiac contractility raising myocardial oxygen demand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of CYP3A4 that accelerates nitrate metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia that raises cardiac output and blood pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synergistic increases in cGMP producing profound vasodilation

explanation.summary: Nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors act synergistically to raise cGMP, causing profound vasodilation and hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide and raise cGMP, while PDE-5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown. Together they act synergistically to cause significant vasodilation and ultimately dramatic reductions in blood pressure, so the two classes should never be taken at the same time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both drugs cause vasodilation, not coronary vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The interaction lowers blood pressure through vasodilation; it does not primarily increase cardiac contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The dangerous effect is a pharmacodynamic synergy on cGMP and blood pressure, not accelerated nitrate metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hallmark of this interaction is hypotension from vasodilation, not a compensatory rise in blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man taking a PDE-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction reports new indigestion and a burning sensation of acid coming back up into his throat. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delayed gastric emptying causing food to remain in the stomach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct erosion of the gastric mucosa by the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased secretion of gastric acid by parietal cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of cGMP within the gastric wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

explanation.summary: Dyspepsia from PDE-5 inhibitors results from relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and acid reflux.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDE-5 inhibitors relax smooth muscle, including the lower esophageal sphincter. This relaxation allows gastric acid to reflux into the esophagus, producing dyspepsia (indigestion or upset stomach).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes dyspepsia to lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, not delayed gastric emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism is smooth muscle relaxation and reflux, not direct erosion of the gastric mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dyspepsia here is due to reflux from sphincter relaxation, not increased acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The symptom results from smooth muscle relaxation permitting reflux, not from local overproduction of cGMP in the stomach.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man who took a PDE-5 inhibitor several hours ago now has a painful erection that has persisted for more than 4 hours. This finding represents which of the following adverse effects, for which he should seek prompt medical attention?

explanation.summary: An erection lasting more than 4 hours is priapism, a medical emergency requiring prompt attention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients taking PDE-5 inhibitors should be aware of priapism, an erection lasting over 4 hours. If this occurs the patient should seek medical attention, as it often requires a procedure to drain blood from the corpus cavernosum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dyspepsia is indigestion from lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, not a prolonged erection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysuria (painful urination) is not the adverse effect described and is not a recognized effect of these drugs here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushing is a common mild vasodilatory effect, not a prolonged painful erection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypotension is low blood pressure from vasodilation, unrelated to the duration of an erection.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with chronic stable angina and a prior myocardial infarction takes isosorbide mononitrate 60 mg daily. At a follow-up visit he reports erectile dysfunction over the past year and asks about medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start any PDE-5 inhibitor as long as it is separated from the nitrate by 2 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start sildenafil at a low dose taken at the same time as his nitrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start tadalafil because its long half-life makes it safest with nitrates

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start vardenafil since it is not affected by fatty meals and avoids interactions

explanation.summary: PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated in patients receiving any form of nitrate due to profound hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDE-5 inhibitors and nitrates act synergistically to cause dramatic reductions in blood pressure. Because this patient takes isosorbide mononitrate, PDE-5 inhibitors should not be prescribed; they must not be used concurrently with any form of nitrate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A 2-hour separation is insufficient; no PDE-5 inhibitor should be used within 24 hours of nitrate therapy, and longer for tadalafil.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Taking sildenafil at the same time as a nitrate is exactly the dangerous combination that must be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tadalafil is not safer with nitrates; its prolonged half-life actually means an even longer interval is needed before a nitrate can be given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The food effect is irrelevant; vardenafil is still contraindicated with nitrates because of the hypotension risk.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man who takes sildenafil is prescribed clarithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic that inhibits CYP3A4, for a respiratory infection. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this combination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete inactivation of sildenafil before it reaches the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of sildenafil into an active nitrate metabolite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced or prolonged sildenafil effect due to reduced metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: No interaction because sildenafil is eliminated only by the kidneys

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced sildenafil effect due to enzyme induction

explanation.summary: CYP3A4 inhibitors reduce metabolism of sildenafil, enhancing or prolonging its effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil are metabolized via CYP3A4, and their effects may be enhanced or prolonged in patients who receive inhibitors of this enzyme. Macrolide antibiotics such as clarithromycin are common CYP3A4 inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibiting CYP3A4 increases drug exposure rather than inactivating the drug before it reaches the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PDE-5 inhibitors are not converted into nitrate metabolites; the interaction is a reduction in metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although renal dose adjustment applies, sildenafil is metabolized by CYP3A4, so this metabolic interaction is clinically important.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A CYP3A4 inhibitor slows metabolism and increases drug levels; it does not induce the enzyme or reduce the effect.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease needs treatment for erectile dysfunction. His physician notes that all PDE-5 inhibitors are eliminated renally and require dose adjustment, but one is of particular concern for toxicity from accumulation because of its prolonged half-life. Which drug is this?

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of them require renal dose adjustment

explanation.summary: Tadalafil's long half-life makes it the most concerning for accumulation and toxicity in renal impairment.
explanation.whyCorrect: All PDE-5 inhibitors are eliminated renally, so doses must be lowered when renal function is decreased. Tadalafil, because of its long half-life, is the most concerning for toxicity due to accumulation in patients with altered kidney function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Avanafil has a duration of about 6 hours and a rapid onset; it is not the primary accumulation concern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All of the PDE-5 inhibitors are eliminated renally and require dose reduction in renal impairment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sildenafil has a much shorter duration of action (about 4 hours) and is less prone to accumulation than tadalafil.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vardenafil has a duration of about 7 hours and is not the drug singled out for accumulation risk.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who frequently eats high-fat meals wants a PDE-5 inhibitor whose absorption will not be reduced by fatty food. Which of the following best fits this requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All PDE-5 inhibitors are equally reduced by fatty meals

explanation.summary: Among the four PDE-5 inhibitors, only tadalafil's absorption is not affected by a fatty meal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the comparison of PDE-5 inhibitors, the absorption of sildenafil, vardenafil, and avanafil is reduced by fatty meals, whereas tadalafil is not affected by fatty meals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tadalafil is the exception whose absorption is not reduced by fatty meals, so they are not all equal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Avanafil absorption is reduced by a fatty meal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sildenafil absorption is reduced by a fatty meal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vardenafil absorption is reduced by a fatty meal.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man starting a PDE-5 inhibitor asks what side effects he is most likely to notice. Which of the following are the most common adverse effects of this drug class, all caused by vasodilation?

explanation.summary: The most common adverse effects of PDE-5 inhibitors are headache, flushing, and dizziness from vasodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Similar to the nitrate medications, the most common adverse effects associated with PDE-5 inhibitors are headache, flushing, and dizziness, all resulting from the vasodilation these drugs cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bradycardia, constipation, and dry mouth are not the vasodilatory effects described for PDE-5 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cough and bronchospasm are not the common adverse effects taught for this class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PDE-5 inhibitors cause hypotension rather than hypertension because of vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weight gain, edema, and hyperglycemia are not associated with PDE-5 inhibitors in this brick.

questions.stem: Before its use in erectile dysfunction was discovered, sildenafil was first studied and used as a mainstay of treatment for another condition, with erections noted as a side effect during those trials. For which condition was sildenafil originally studied?

explanation.summary: Sildenafil was first studied for pulmonary arterial hypertension, where its erectile side effect was noticed.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDE-5 inhibitors are a mainstay of treatment for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Sildenafil was first studied for this indication, and male patients were found to experience erections as a side effect, which led to its use in erectile dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is not the original indication described for sildenafil in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic stable angina is treated with nitrates, not with the original sildenafil indication described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Congestive heart failure is not the condition for which sildenafil was first studied.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sildenafil was studied for pulmonary arterial hypertension, not essential systemic hypertension.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is given a cholinergic agonist during a study of autonomic reflexes, and his heart rate slows. Activation of which of the following signaling pathways in cardiac tissue is most directly responsible for this effect?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gq-coupled receptor that increases IP3 and intracellular calcium

explanation.summary: Cardiac slowing by cholinergics is mediated by the M2 receptor, a Gi-coupled GPCR that lowers cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the heart, muscarinic M2 receptors couple to Gi, decreasing cAMP and reducing rate and AV nodal conduction. This is why parasympathetic (cholinergic) activation slows the pulse.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq with increased IP3/Ca2+ is the M1/M3 pathway for glands and smooth muscle, not the cardiac slowing pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gs increases cAMP and would raise, not lower, heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligand-gated Na+/K+ channels describe nicotinic (Nm) receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not cardiac muscarinic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic receptors are GPCRs, not tyrosine kinase receptors.

questions.stem: Which muscarinic receptor subtype is primarily responsible for slowing the heart rate and impulse conduction through the cardiac nodes?

explanation.summary: The M2 receptor mediates cholinergic slowing of the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: M2 is the dominant cardiac muscarinic receptor; via Gi it decreases cAMP and slows the pulse rate and conduction through the SA and AV nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M1 is a Gq neuronal receptor associated with cognition, memory, and learning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M3 is a Gq receptor driving gland secretion and smooth-muscle contraction, not cardiac slowing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M5 is not the clinically important cardiac subtype; M1-M3 are the key clinical receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nm is the nicotinic ligand-gated channel at skeletal muscle, unrelated to nodal slowing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man cannot void on the third postoperative day. There is no mechanical obstruction, and his bladder is markedly distended. A drug is chosen that contracts the detrusor muscle and relaxes the internal urethral sphincter to promote emptying. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Bethanechol is the direct-acting cholinergic used to treat non-obstructive urinary retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bethanechol is an orally administered choline ester that causes bladder detrusor contraction and relaxes the urinary sphincter, treating urinary retention (and also ileus).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase and is not used therapeutically for retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atropine is an antimuscarinic; it relaxes the detrusor and would worsen retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbachol is used ophthalmically for glaucoma, not for bladder emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma, not urinary retention.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome has severe dry mouth that is also worse after prior head and neck radiation. She is started on an oral agent that stimulates salivary secretion. Which of the following was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine is used orally to treat xerostomia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine, a tertiary-amine alkaloid, is used for xerostomia after head and neck radiation and in Sjogren syndrome, where disrupted lacrimal and salivary function improves with cholinergic stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic that would reduce secretions and worsen dry mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not xerostomia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is used as ophthalmic drops for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methacholine is a diagnostic bronchoprovocation agent with no other therapeutic use.

questions.stem: A patient with glaucoma is treated with cholinergic eye drops. The reduction in intraocular pressure is best explained by which of the following drug-induced effects?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxation of the bladder detrusor muscle

explanation.summary: Cholinergic drops lower intraocular pressure by contracting the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbachol and pilocarpine cause miosis by contracting the pupillary sphincter and adjust the ciliary muscle, reducing resistance to aqueous humor outflow and thereby lowering intraocular pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics cause bronchoconstriction, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholinergics increase, not decrease, lacrimal secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis; mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bladder effects are unrelated to the ocular mechanism of pressure reduction.

questions.stem: Indirect-acting cholinomimetic agents increase parasympathetic activity through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking reuptake of norepinephrine at the synapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly binding and activating muscarinic receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing synthesis of choline in the presynaptic neuron

explanation.summary: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics are cholinesterase inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike direct-acting agents that bind receptors, indirect-acting cholinomimetics inhibit acetylcholinesterase, preventing breakdown of ACh and thereby increasing PNS activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors would reduce, not increase, cholinergic transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking norepinephrine reuptake is an adrenergic action unrelated to cholinergic breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That describes direct-acting cholinomimetics, not the indirect class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing choline synthesis is not the defined mechanism of these drugs.

questions.stem: Compared with acetylcholine, choline ester drugs such as carbachol have a longer duration of action. Which of the following properties best explains this difference?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible covalent binding to the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid renal excretion of the active drug

explanation.summary: Choline esters are longer-acting because they resist acetylcholinesterase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Modification of the choline side chain makes esters like carbachol more resistant to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase than ACh, giving a longer duration of action. Methacholine is the exception, being rapidly hydrolyzed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs do bind and activate muscarinic receptors, which is required for their effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Their action is receptor activation, not irreversible covalent binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rapid hydrolysis would shorten, not lengthen, duration; this describes ACh (and methacholine).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Duration is explained by enzymatic resistance, not renal excretion in this brick.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with intermittent cough and suspected asthma undergoes pulmonary function testing. An inhaled agent is administered to provoke bronchoconstriction as a diagnostic challenge. Which of the following was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Methacholine is used for bronchoprovocation testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methacholine is indicated for testing bronchospastic (bronchoprovocation) activity as a diagnostic tool and, unlike the other choline esters, is rapidly hydrolyzed and has no other therapeutic use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic and would block, not provoke, bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not bronchial testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is an ophthalmic agent for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma.

questions.stem: Activation of muscarinic receptors in the gastrointestinal tract produces which of the following effects?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of the internal anal sphincter

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation increases GI motility and secretions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic (M3) activation increases gastric motility and secretions and relaxes the internal anal sphincter; the increased motility can cause diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased motility, not decreased, is the cholinergic effect, so constipation is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The internal anal sphincter relaxes rather than contracts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric secretions increase with cholinergic activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salivation increases with cholinergic activation.

questions.stem: Cholinergic activation of the eye produces which of the following effects?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation of the eye causes miosis and ciliary contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic activation contracts the sphincter and ciliary muscles of the eye, producing miosis (pupil constriction) and increased lacrimation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation increases lacrimation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic drugs lower intraocular pressure, which is why they treat glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect, the opposite of cholinergic action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pupillary sphincter contracts, not relaxes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome is treated with oral pilocarpine. Which of the following adverse effects is she most likely to report, occurring in roughly half of patients?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine commonly causes excessive sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine is associated with excess sweating; about 50-60% of patients report this adverse effect due to cholinergic stimulation of sweat glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics increase GI motility and tend toward diarrhea, not constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergics increase secretions and sweating, so dry skin is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic activation slows the heart, producing bradycardia rather than tachycardia.

questions.stem: Pilocarpine differs from choline ester cholinergics in that it is a tertiary-amine alkaloid. Which of the following properties does this structure confer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only be administered intravenously

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is rapidly degraded by acetylcholinesterase

explanation.summary: As a tertiary-amine alkaloid, pilocarpine crosses the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that pilocarpine is a tertiary amine that does cross the blood-brain barrier, distinguishing it from the choline esters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pilocarpine is given orally and ophthalmically, not only IV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist and does activate these receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its alkaloid structure is not a substrate rapidly cleaved by acetylcholinesterase like ACh.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine acts on muscarinic receptors, not selectively on nicotinic receptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist is describing how a class of drugs produces its effects. The drugs bind muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the peripheral nervous system and CNS but leave nicotinic receptors unaffected, and their actions are opposite to those of the rest-and-digest parasympathetic system. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of these drugs?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics (antimuscarinics) act by competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that anticholinergics act primarily through competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors in the PNS, CNS, or both, and that most do not block nicotinic receptors. Their effects are therefore opposite to those of parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergics target muscarinic, not adrenergic, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They antagonize rather than activate muscarinic receptors; agonism would produce cholinergic (parasympathetic) effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase raises acetylcholine and produces cholinergic effects, the opposite of an anticholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticholinergics generally do not block nicotinic receptors, and their muscarinic blockade is competitive and reversible.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in the emergency department has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 38/min and lightheadedness. He is given intravenous atropine, and his heart rate rises to 74/min. Blockade of which receptor best explains this increase in heart rate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: M2 muscarinic receptors on the heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on glandular tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: Atropine speeds the heart by blocking cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors, removing vagal slowing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's organ table lists the heart's effect as increased heart rate mediated by M2 receptors. Anticholinergics inhibit the parasympathetic (vagal) slowing of the heart, producing tachycardia, which is why atropine is useful in symptomatic bradycardia and AV node block.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist and does not act on beta-1 adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Airway M3 receptors govern bronchial tone, not cardiac rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors on glands mediate secretions (dry mouth), not heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuromuscular nicotinic receptors control skeletal muscle, not the heart rate, and are not blocked by atropine.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is planning a week-long ocean cruise and reports severe seasickness on prior trips. Her physician prescribes a transdermal patch that must be replaced after 72 hours. Which anticholinergic drug is most likely being prescribed?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine, a transdermal-patch anticholinergic, is used for motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states scopolamine (hyoscine) is usually formulated as a transdermal patch to treat motion sickness and postsurgical nausea, and that the patches are not for continuous use and should be replaced after 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is used for bradycardia, reducing secretions, and as a poisoning antidote, not as a motion-sickness patch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats urinary urge incontinence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop used to dilate the pupil.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD is prescribed an inhaled anticholinergic to add to his beta-agonist and inhaled corticosteroid. By blocking M3 receptors in the airways, this drug relieves his symptoms. Which effect on the airways is responsible for the benefit?

explanation.summary: Inhaled anticholinergics such as ipratropium cause bronchodilation and reduce mucus secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that M3 receptors in the lungs can cause bronchoconstriction; blocking them with ipratropium or tiotropium reduces mucus secretions and bronchoconstriction, lowering airway resistance and allowing easier breathing in asthma and COPD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoconstriction and increased secretions are the parasympathetic effects that anticholinergics oppose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The benefit comes from bronchodilation and decreased secretions, not increased ciliary clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surfactant production is not a described mechanism of these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the effect to airway smooth muscle and secretions, not pulmonary vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a sudden, frequent urge to urinate with occasional involuntary leakage, and urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity. She is started on oxybutynin. What is the mechanism by which this drug relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck and trigone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking muscarinic receptors to slow detrusor contractions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing urine production through a renal diuretic effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxing the internal urethral sphincter to ease voiding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating detrusor muscle contraction to empty the bladder

explanation.summary: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic that slows detrusor contractions to control urge incontinence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes oxybutynin as the prototypical anticholinergic for urinary incontinence (overactive bladder); by blocking M3 receptors it slows bladder detrusor contractions, helping patients control urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxybutynin is antimuscarinic, not an alpha-adrenergic blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drug does not increase urine production; it reduces involuntary bladder contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics reduce detrusor overactivity; they do not work by relaxing the urethral sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating detrusor contraction would worsen urgency and leakage.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupil to examine the retina during a funduscopic exam. Which of the following anticholinergic agents, administered as an eye drop, is most appropriate for producing mydriasis?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic drops such as tropicamide (or atropine) dilate the pupil for eye exams.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine and tropicamide drops are used to dilate the pupil for ophthalmoscopic exams; the mydriasis helps with retinal and pupillary examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate does not penetrate well and is not described as an ophthalmic mydriatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats overactive bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used as a transdermal patch for motion sickness, not as an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A toxicology instructor teaches the classic anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic. A poisoned patient who is described as 'mad as a hatter' is exhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased secretions, dry mouth, and thirst

explanation.summary: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to the CNS effects of anticholinergic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick maps 'mad as a hatter' to central nervous system effects such as drowsiness, hallucinations, and coma, which result from central muscarinic blockade in agents that penetrate the CNS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry mouth and decreased secretions correspond to 'dry as a bone'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushed skin corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis and blurred vision correspond to 'blind as a bat'.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tachycardia (and overheating) corresponds to 'hot as a hare'.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with severe lower abdominal pain and states he has not urinated in several days. He has no prior urinary problems and is generally healthy but recently began an over-the-counter allergy medicine for a runny nose. Examination reveals a markedly distended bladder requiring catheterization. Which property of his allergy medication best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains diphenhydramine with anticholinergic properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a direct cholinergic agonist that stimulates the detrusor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a diuretic that overfilled the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that relaxes the bladder neck

explanation.summary: OTC diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties that can cause urinary retention, especially in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case describes exactly this scenario: the allergy medicine contains diphenhydramine, an antihistamine with anticholinergic properties. By blocking muscarinic receptors it decreases detrusor contraction and causes urinary retention, a particular risk in elderly patients who also face confusion, constipation, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cholinergic agonist would promote urination, not cause retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A diuretic would increase urine output; the problem was inability to void due to anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor increases acetylcholine and cholinergic activity, opposite to what caused retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-blockade at the bladder neck would ease urine flow, not cause retention.

questions.stem: A patient who took a large amount of an anticholinergic agent is brought to the emergency department. On the anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic, the finding 'dry as a bone' reflects which underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone at M2 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cutaneous vasodilation in the skin vasculature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased gut motility with delayed transit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupillary dilation from iris sphincter blockade

explanation.summary: 'Dry as a bone' reflects inhibition of secretions, producing dry mouth, dry eyes, and decreased sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick attributes 'dry as a bone' to the general inhibition of secretions in mucous membranes and skin, giving dry mouth, dry eyes, and reduced sweating from muscarinic blockade of exocrine glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone produces tachycardia ('hot as a hare').
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous flushing corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased gut motility contributes to 'full as a flask' (retention/constipation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation corresponds to 'blind as a bat'.

questions.stem: A farm worker is brought in after exposure to an organophosphate insecticide, with copious secretions, bradycardia, and pinpoint pupils. Which anticholinergic drug is the appropriate antidote for this acetylcholine-excess (muscarinic) toxicity?

explanation.summary: Atropine is the antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, such as organophosphate or muscarine poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states atropine is an antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, including poisoning by organophosphates or muscarine-containing wild mushrooms. By competitively blocking muscarinic receptors, it reverses the excess-cholinergic secretions, bradycardia, and miosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin is a bladder-selective agent for overactive bladder, not a poisoning antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used for motion sickness, not as the antidote of choice for cholinergic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A student is asked to predict adverse effects of anticholinergic drugs from their receptor actions. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of an anticholinergic agent?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics decrease GI motility, which can lead to constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review question confirms constipation as a correct answer: anticholinergics inhibit gut smooth muscle contraction and decrease motility, which can cause constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They cause tachycardia by blocking vagal tone, not bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They decrease, not increase, GI motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease secretions, causing dry mouth, not increased salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They cause mydriasis (dilation), not miosis.

questions.stem: A neurologist notes that some antimuscarinic drugs are useful for CNS diseases while others are not, depending on how well they penetrate the brain. Which of the following best explains why ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are NOT useful in treating Parkinson disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are direct dopamine receptor antagonists in the striatum

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are rapidly metabolized in the gut wall before they are absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: They block nicotinic rather than muscarinic receptors in the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: They do not adequately cross into the central nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate rather than block muscarinic receptors centrally

explanation.summary: CNS penetration varies among antimuscarinics; poorly penetrating agents cannot treat central diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that muscarinic antagonists have variable CNS penetration. Certain agents (e.g., benztropine, atropine) carry greater CNS effects, whereas ipratropium and glycopyrrolate do not penetrate the CNS well and therefore are not useful in treating CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are antimuscarinics, not dopamine antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the difference to CNS penetration, not to pre-absorption metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs are muscarinic antagonists; the issue is CNS penetration, not a switch to nicotinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They block, rather than stimulate, muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis takes an over-the-counter H1 antihistamine and notices that her runny nose improves. This symptom relief is most directly explained by which of the following actions of the drug on endothelial cells adjacent to vascular smooth muscle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of mast cell degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide and prostacyclin release

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines reduce nasal symptoms by blocking H1 receptors, which inhibits nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produces vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By antagonizing H1 receptors on endothelial cells, the drug inhibits the release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin. This causes vasoconstriction and reduces edema formation, lessening runny nose symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 antihistamines act on histamine receptors, not nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gastric acid secretion is a function of H2 blockers, not H1 antihistamines used for allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor; they do not trigger mast cell degranulation, which is what releases histamine in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased nitric oxide and prostacyclin would cause vasodilation and worsen edema, the opposite of the drug's effect.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes diphenhydramine for allergies and becomes very drowsy, while his coworker taking loratadine for the same allergies reports no sedation. Which property of diphenhydramine best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and cannot enter the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively blocks H2 receptors in the stomach

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier, blocking central H1 receptors and causing sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they block central H1 receptors that normally promote wakefulness, producing drowsiness. Second-generation drugs like loratadine are hydrophilic and penetrate the brain poorly, so they are non-sedating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, not a second-generation, antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that is precisely why it enters the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphenhydramine blocks H1, not H2 receptors, and H2 blockade would not explain sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug blocks H1 receptors; it does not stimulate central histamine release.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a non-sedating antihistamine for chronic urticaria so that daytime alertness is preserved. Which of the following agents best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine are non-sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine. These agents are hydrophilic, act primarily on peripheral H1 receptors, and cause little sedation, making them ideal when alertness must be preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent that causes marked drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine and is sedating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is a first-generation agent with sedating and antimuscarinic properties.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought in for confusion, blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty urinating that began after he started an over-the-counter first-generation antihistamine. These findings are best explained by the drug's action at which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Many first-generation antihistamines also block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines have antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) activity. Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and, especially in the elderly, confusion and delirium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2 blockade relates to bronchial and vascular tone, not dry mouth and urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects, not the dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 receptors regulate gastric acid; blocking them does not cause this anticholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptor blockade would affect the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, not this pattern of anticholinergic findings.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has persistent nausea and vomiting. Her physician prescribes doxylamine in combination with which of the following, an FDA-approved regimen for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Doxylamine plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an approved treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxylamine, a first-generation antihistamine, combined with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), is approved for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. First-generation agents cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects but is not the antiemetic partner of doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 is used for pernicious anemia, not paired with doxylamine for pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not part of this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D addresses bone and calcium metabolism, not nausea of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A family planning a road trip asks for a medication to prevent motion sickness in an adult. Which antihistamine is most appropriate, and what property makes it effective for this indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cetirizine, because it is hydrophilic and non-sedating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desloratadine, because it blocks H2 receptors in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fexofenadine, because it acts only at peripheral sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loratadine, because it is non-sedating and long acting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promethazine, because of its antimuscarinic properties

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines with antimuscarinic activity, such as promethazine, are effective against motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that first-generation antihistamines like promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties that make them effective in treating motion sickness. Second-generation agents lack this activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent lacking meaningful antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desloratadine is an H1, not H2, agent and is second-generation; it is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fexofenadine acts only peripherally and is not used for motion sickness.
